lead: The covenant with Abram is sealed in the dark, and only God passes between the pieces. The promise rests on his faithfulness. Paul, who knew that faithfulness, still says: “I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:14). In the Gospel Jesus asks the question each disciple must answer, and Peter replies. On the day our Church gives thanks for its rank as a Major Archiepiscopal Church, these readings set both the gift and the task before us.

r.h: The fire passes between the pieces
set: This closes the scene that began at 15:7. Abram asked how he could know, the animals were cut in two, and he fell into a deep sleep. Jeremiah 34:18 shows what passing between the parts meant: those who walked between them called on themselves the fate of the slain animal if they broke their word. Now comes the surprise. Abram does not walk. Only the fire passes, and fire and smoke will later mark God's presence at the Exodus and at Sinai (Exodus 13:21; 19:18).
str: v. 17: at nightfall the fire pot and the torch pass between the pieces.
v. 18: “On that day” the Lord makes the covenant and states the gift.
vv. 19–21: a list of ten peoples of the land.
kw: A tannûr is a clay oven or fire pot. The POC has തീച്ചൂള. Smoke and flame are all that this passage shows of God.
The same word lappîd appears in the plural at Sinai for the flashes seen by the people (Exodus 20:18).
The Hebrew idiom is literally “to cut a covenant”, which is why the cutting of the animals belongs to the story.
vv: When the sun had gone down and it was dark, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.
Many commentators see here the heart of the chapter: God binds himself alone. Abram contributes nothing except the waiting.
On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram
The word “covenant” joins the promise of land to the God who has just passed between the pieces in the fire. Abram is still childless and still owns none of this land. All of it is given by word.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews draws on this kind of oath: “When God made a promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself” (Hebrews 6:13). St Paul says that the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and the Church honours the covenant with Israel, which God has not revoked (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4). For Christians the line runs on to the Upper Room: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). What God took on himself in figure in the dark of Genesis, Christ fulfils on the Cross, and we receive at every Holy Qurbono.

r.h: But who do you say that I am?
set: Herod has just asked, “who is this about whom I hear such things?” (9:9), and Jesus has fed the five thousand (9:10–17). Now comes the answer. Luke tells this more briefly than Mark (8:27–30) and Matthew (16:13–20). He does not name Caesarea Philippi, but he alone says that Jesus was praying. The next verses, beyond today's reading, bring the first prediction of the Passion (9:21–22), so the title must be understood through the Cross.
str: v. 18: Jesus at prayer; the question about the crowds.
v. 19: their answers: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the ancient prophets.
v. 20: the question to the disciples; Peter's confession.
kw: Luke often shows Jesus at prayer at the great turning points: the baptism (3:21), the choosing of the Twelve (6:12), the Transfiguration (9:28–29). Peter's confession comes out of that prayer.
The Greek places “you” first for emphasis. Others' opinions are heard, and then each disciple is asked directly.
Christos is the Greek for the Hebrew māšîaḥ, the anointed one. “Of God” says who anointed him and to whom he belongs.
vv: Who do the crowds say that I am?
The crowds are not hostile. They place Jesus among the great figures of the past. That is respectful, and it is not enough.
But who do you say that I am?
This question cannot be answered by reporting what others say. It is put to every generation.
Peter speaks for the Twelve and says the true thing, though he does not yet know the road it will take.
ch: The Catechism says: “On the rock of this faith confessed by St. Peter, Christ built his Church” (CCC 424), and teaches that Peter holds the first place in the college of the Twelve because of the confession the Father revealed to him (CCC 552). What Peter says in the name of all, each Christian says personally in baptism and in the Creed.

rite: On 10 February 2005 Pope John Paul II raised the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church to the rank of a Major Archiepiscopal Church, with Moran Mor Cyril Baselios as the first Major Archbishop. This Church grew from the reunion led by Mar Ivanios in 1930. It keeps its own West Syriac, Antiochene liturgy and lives in full communion with the Bishop of Rome. Today's Gospel fits the day: the confession of Peter is the faith we share with the whole Church, and we say it in our own tradition's voice. Let us give thanks, and pray with respect and love for all our sister Churches of the Malankara tradition.
study: God bound himself alone while Abram slept. Where do I still act as if God's faithfulness depended on my own?
If Jesus asked me today, “who do you say that I am?”, what would I answer in my own words? How does my life answer it?
